Kindergarten · Unit K-C

Living Things and Their Homes

What do living things need, and how do homes and helpers support them?

You did this before / what is new. You noticed sunlight and water in K-B; now you connect needs to homes, see how living things change places, and take one real helper action.

Concept 1

Plants and animals have needs

Plants and animals need things such as water, air, food, sunlight, and space to survive.

Analogy

A needs list for a plant and a needs list for an animal.

“Plants need water and sunlight. Animals need food, water, and air.”

Try it

Sort living things and nonliving things; then match needs cards.

“Does it need water?”

Data

Needs chart for a bean plant and a deer.

“Bean: water, sunlight, air. Deer: food, water, air.”

Real world

Michigan robins eat worms, drink water, and need safe places.

“Robins need food and water.”

Concept 2

Homes meet needs

A habitat provides food, water, shelter, and space; different habitats have different living things.

Diagram

Pond, forest, and sand dune.

“A pond gives fish water.”

Try it

Sort Michigan animals into habitats.

“Where does the frog live?”

Try it

Build a habitat model with clay, paper, and blue paper water.

“My model has water, shelter, and food.”

Data

Count different living things in habitat pictures.

“Forest had 6 kinds.”

Real world

Great Lakes shores have water, sand, plants, birds, and insects.

“The shore is a home.”

Concept 3

Living things change their environment

Living things change their surroundings to meet needs.

Diagram

Beaver dam blocking a stream.

“Beavers make dams.”

Try it

Look at evidence cards: beaver dam, worm tunnels, bird nest, dog digging, squirrel with acorns.

“Did a living thing change this place?”

Data

Class argument chart: Place changed? Evidence.

“I see tunnels. A worm changed the soil.”

Real world

People build houses and roads.

“People change land too.”

Concept 4

People can reduce harm

People can make choices that help local land, water, air, and living things.

Analogy

Helper hands.

“We can be habitat helpers.”

Try it

Choose one real local action: schoolyard litter pick or planting a native flower.

“We pick up litter. We take a before photo and an after photo.”

Data

Before/after photo or tally chart.

“Before: 10 litter pieces. After: 0.”

Real world

Native flowers help bees and butterflies.

“Native flowers help bees.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Habitat Helper Action. Students choose a local habitat problem, such as litter near the schoolyard or lack of pollinator plants. They carry out one real action: a supervised litter pick with before/after photos or planting a native flower. They draw a habitat model and say how their action helps land, water, air, or living things.

Try it

What you need

Michigan plant and animal pictures, bean plant or bean plant photo, paper, crayons, clay or play dough, blue paper for water, evidence cards, tape, gloves for litter pick, camera or drawing sheet for before/after evidence.

Safety: Wash hands after soil, sand, plants, or outdoor litter work. Adults help with litter pickup; do not touch sharp objects. No coin cells or magnets are needed.

Try it

What you do

Match needs to living things, build habitat models, sort evidence cards to argue how living things change places, and complete one real local helper action.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but the standard expects you to collect your own when you can.

If you cannot grow or observe a bean plant, use this chart: bean plant needs water, sunlight, air, and space; deer needs food, water, air, and space. Habitat picture counts: pond = 4 kinds of living things, forest = 6 kinds, sand dune = 3 kinds. Evidence cards: beaver dam, worm tunnels, bird nest, squirrel acorns, dog dig. Before/after sample: litter pieces before = 10, after = 0.

Near you: White-tailed deer, robins, trout, beavers, maple trees, milkweed, Great Lakes habitats, dunes, forests, and schoolyard native plantings.

Words to know

living thing
a plant, animal, or other organism.
need
something required to live or grow.
habitat
home that gives needs.
shelter
a safe place to live.
environment
the place around a living thing.
change
make something different.
reduce
make less.
native
naturally from a place.
evidence
what we see that helps answer.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, standards, pacing

Pacing: 5 sessions of 30 minutes.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Plants eat soil.” Correct: plants need water, light, and air; soil holds the plant in place and gives it water and minerals.
  • “Plants need only dirt.” Correct: plants also need water, sunlight, air, and space.
  • “A habitat is only where an animal sleeps.” Correct: a habitat provides food, water, shelter, and space.
  • “Living things do not change their environment.” Correct: organisms can change their surroundings.
  • “Only people change the environment.” Correct: animals and plants can change environments too.
  • “People cannot help nature.” Correct: local actions can reduce harm.
  • “Litter does not harm habitats.” Correct: litter can harm land, water, and living things.

Limits and cautions:

  • K-ESS3-3 is only partial unless students complete one real local action with evidence.
  • Litter picks need adult supervision, gloves, and permission. Do not touch sharp objects.
  • If planting is not possible, use a photo dataset and a classroom “before/after” simulation, but note that real action gives the strongest evidence.
  • This unit does not cover external parts, biomimicry, parent-offspring behavior, or young resembling parents; those belong in 1-B and 2-B.
  • Food needs are simplified; ecosystems are more complex and are developed later in 5.3.

Michigan Science Standards this unit earns:

  • K-LS1-1: Use observations to describe patterns of what plants and animals need to survive. Fully addressed with needs charts, sorting, and evidence cards.
  • K-ESS3-1: Use a model to show the relationship between the needs of plants or animals and the places they live. Fully addressed with habitat models.
  • K-ESS2-2: Observe and discuss how living things change their environment. Fully addressed with evidence cards and a class argument.
  • K-ESS3-3: Communicate solutions that reduce the impact of humans on the land, water, air, and other living things in the local environment. Partly addressed if only discussed; fully addressed when students complete one real local action with before/after evidence.

Connections: - Builds on: K2.0 Science Noticing and Asking if taught; K-B Sunlight, Weather, and Staying Safe for sunlight and water. - Builds toward: 1-B Parts, Parents, and Young, 2-B Plants, Animals, and Habitats, 3.3 Life Cycles and Traits, 3.4 Survival, Fossils, and Change, 5.3 Energy and Matter in Ecosystems, 6 Unit 7: Cells, 6 Unit 8: Classifying Life, 6 Unit 12: Ecosystems & Food Webs, and 7.5 Photosynthesis & Matter Cycling.
